source.title: Overfitting in adversarially robust deep learning
source.authors: L. Rice; Eric Wong; J. Kolter

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure content is represented only by plots, but the text and tables report the principal results.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that training longer can worsen robust test performance, while increasing architecture size can improve it; it explicitly distinguishes this behavior from standard training and says the robust overfitting is not explained by double descent. These results concern adversarial robustness, outside the versions’ standard-training conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper studies adversarially trained models and robust error under adversarial attacks. That differs from the claim’s standard training on natural labels. Its comparisons to standard error are reported alongside robust-training experiments, not as tests of the listed standard-training versions. Results cited from other studies were not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures robust overfitting, width effects and mitigation under adversarial training. These results concern a different outcome and training regime from V1–V8. Its standard-error checkpoint comparisons do not test any version's named comparison either. Discussion of ordinary generalization and dropout supplies background, not tests.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. Robust overfitting occurs across many adversarial-training settings; wider architectures improve robust performance without eliminating it. The evaluated regularizers and augmentations in isolation do not significantly improve upon early stopping. Semi-supervised augmentation combined with early stopping improves further, and the authors recommend validation-based model selection.
record.recipe_differences: Adversarial training optimizes against input perturbations and evaluates robust error under specified attacks; the claim versions concern standard training on natural labels and ordinary held-out test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Robust test outcomes vary with dataset, perturbation norm and radius, training algorithm, architecture width, learning-rate schedule, checkpoint timing, regularization, augmentation and whether early stopping is used. The default TRADES learning-rate schedule on the smaller pre-activation ResNet18 was the one of four schedule/architecture combinations that did not show clear degradation; the authors attribute this to shortened training and smaller capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Robust test error deteriorates after its best checkpoint across several adversarial-training settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarially trained classifiers can exhibit increasing robust test error while robust training performance continues to improve.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider adversarially trained Wide ResNets improve robust test error while retaining robust overfitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width can improve adversarial robustness without eliminating deterioration from continued training; the observed double-descent peak precedes robust interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation-based early stopping is competitive with the tested regularizers and augmentations; semi-supervised augmentation combined with checkpoint selection improves further.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested CIFAR-10 adversarial-training setup, the evaluated alternatives in isolation do not significantly improve upon early stopping, whereas semi-supervised augmentation with early stopping does.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning-rate schedules affect robust-error curves and the best checkpoint obtained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested smoother schedules have worse best robust test error than piecewise decay, and tuning the post-decay learning rate modestly improves the best checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: Some adversarially trained models also exhibit increased ordinary test error during continued training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ordinary test error can deteriorate alongside robust error in the reported CIFAR-100 and ImageNet adversarial-training settings.

record.problems: Many schedule and width comparisons are presented in figures without numeric tables. ImageNet final errors have large reported variation, and the pretrained ℓ∞ ImageNet model's prior training schedule is unclear. The study's robust-error findings use adversarial training and do not directly test the standard-training claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: Most per-model, per-schedule and per-width learning-curve values in Figures 2, 5, 9–30 were not extracted where the text gives no numerical value. Table 5 and Appendix D.2 repeat regularization results; duplicate rows were omitted. Only selected standard-error comparisons were retained because they are explicitly numeric and differ from the robust-error findings.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy under matched recipes.
Ordinary test-error changes beyond the width needed for zero training error in the stated training regime. Robust-error width sweeps are a separate finding.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning, weight decay and optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout's effect, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their version links are none; this does not deny the reported robustness effects. Reported final-error deviations generally describe variation across the last five epochs, not uncertainty across independent training runs. No listed version receives a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under standard training.
Width sweep uses adversarial training and robust error, not standard training and natural-label test error.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison under standard training.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison for standard training.
No large-batch comparison under standard training.
No removal or retraining of memorized examples.
